segments.title: Imperial fleet units were designed for commerce protection
segments.body: The 1909 plan would give Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and other parts of the empire more responsibility for their own sea lanes. A battlecruiser formed the heavy element of a mixed force built for convoy escort, deterrence, and hunting surface raiders such as Vice-Admiral von Spee's East Asia Squadron. New Zealand was prepared to fund and support the China Station formation, but it did not want to supply a wholly New Zealand crew because of its population size. That arrangement produced HMS New Zealand, while Australia operated HMAS Australia. These units were commerce-protection forces and were not intended to engage concentrated enemy navies as compact battle fleets.

evidence.note: The transcript explains the 1909 fleet-unit composition and its commerce-protection, escort, deterrence, and raider-hunting roles.

segments.summary: The 1909 Imperial Conference scheme paired a battlecruiser with cruisers, destroyers, and submarines for trade protection, convoy escort, deterrence, and raider hunting.

segments.title: Canada's stop-start fleet policy slows the 1909 scheme
segments.body: Canada repeatedly reopened its naval options while Australia and New Zealand moved quickly on the 1909 fleet-unit scheme. Its policy could swing between minimal armament and a proposal for three Queen Elizabeth-class battleships. That hesitation supplies the slower procurement timetable needed for the alternate scenario. It also shows how Canada could leap from delay to an unusually large capital-ship proposal instead of building its fleet incrementally.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts Canada's repeated reconsideration and three-Queen-Elizabeth proposal with the rapid Australian and New Zealand decisions.

segments.summary: Canada repeatedly revisits its naval commitment and at one point considers three Queen Elizabeth-class battleships, while Australia and New Zealand place their orders quickly.

segments.title: Lord Dudley drives Australia's rapid naval procurement
segments.body: William Ward, second Earl of Dudley, supplied much of the political drive behind Australia's unusually fast decision. He drew lessons from the Russo-Japanese and Spanish-American wars, especially the exposure created by Australia's coastal population and weak internal communications. His answer was to strengthen local ships and infrastructure before asking the Royal Navy for more support. Dudley then pressed Australian politicians, British industry, the Admiralty, the Treasury, and the Foreign Office to complete the order in December 1909. Moving so many institutions that quickly was his main procurement achievement.

evidence.note: Dudley's strategic reasoning and the speed with which he drove the Australian and British systems are described.

segments.summary: Governor-General Lord Dudley turns the 1909 conference concept into an unusually rapid Australian order and helps pull New Zealand into the scheme.

segments.title: Dudley's political weakness makes a procurement delay plausible
segments.body: Dudley's record in Australia also exposed the limits of his methods. His strained relationship with Labor leader Andrew Fisher made it risky for a governor-general to appear aligned against a major party. Fisher's frugality and socialist background sat uneasily with Dudley's attachment to vice-regal status and ceremony. The regiment Dudley had commanded later went to Egypt and served alongside the ANZACs after he had been seconded away, costing him a possible chance to repair his standing with Australians. Better political restraint could delay the order while leaving the fleet-unit plan intact.

evidence.note: Dudley's political friction, emphasis on status, difficult relationship with Andrew Fisher, and missed chance to serve alongside the ANZACs are described.

segments.summary: Dudley's partisan friction and fondness for vice-regal ceremony give Australian political leaders a plausible way to slow the 1909 order.

segments.title: Why the Indefatigable class had no strong Washington case
segments.body: The historical ships were ordered while the more capable Lion class was already emerging, although overseas bases and support would absorb much of the expense required for larger ships. They could not count on outrunning enemy battlecruisers, and their protection and subdivision offered too little margin once they were forced into battle. Jutland also damaged the type's reputation. Their use in the line of battle was a command and doctrinal failure as well as a design problem, since commerce-protection battlecruisers were never meant to absorb sustained battleship fire. Washington delegates therefore had newer, better-armed British capital ships to retain.

evidence.note: The transcript compares the Indefatigables with Lions and explains their gunnery and survivability weaknesses.
Their Jutland reputation, doctrinal misuse, and lack of treaty-era retention value are assessed.

segments.summary: The Indefatigables' 12-inch guns, limited survivability, older design, and damaged reputation leave Australia and New Zealand with little worth defending at Washington.

segments.title: Delay the orders and build 15-inch-gun Tigers
segments.body: The alternate path requires Dudley to slow down or Australian ministers to exercise more control over the timetable. Once Tiger and the Queen Elizabeth class were shaping British construction, returning to the older Indefatigable design would make little sense. The proposed ships are enlarged Tigers with eight 15-inch guns and somewhat better protection, one each for Australia, New Zealand, and the Royal Navy. The scenario calls this trio the Hood class. Reworking a familiar design keeps the proposal more conservative than starting from a wholly new concept.

evidence.note: A procurement delay leads to three enlarged Tiger-derived battlecruisers with 15-inch guns and improved protection.

segments.summary: A slower Australian decision moves construction from the Indefatigable era to an enlarged Tiger design armed with 15-inch guns.

segments.title: The new battlecruisers reach Jutland
segments.body: Ships ordered alongside the Queen Elizabeth programme would probably miss Dogger Bank and reach service before Jutland. With Queen Elizabeth-class fire control, three modern 15-inch-gun ships would join Tiger, Lion, Princess Royal, Queen Mary, and the surviving 12-inch types in a much stronger fast wing. Their arrival could leave the Queen Elizabeths with the Grand Fleet and move older battlecruisers to training or less decisive duties. Credible performance at Jutland would later give politicians a concrete wartime reason to retain fast capital ships.

evidence.note: The transcript places the three 15-inch-gun ships in service before Jutland and considers how they change Grand Fleet assignments.
Their fire control and the resulting mix of 15-inch, 13.5-inch, and 12-inch battlecruisers are set out.

segments.summary: Three 15-inch-gun battlecruisers could enter service after Dogger Bank but before Jutland, reshaping the Grand Fleet's fast wing and wartime building choices.

segments.title: Battlecruiser orders preserve the battleship programme
segments.body: The alternate orders could preserve all eight Revenge-class and six Queen Elizabeth-class battleships. Fisher historically argued for pausing battleship construction while pursuing the large light cruisers Courageous, Glorious, and Furious. The claim that cancellations would preserve repair space does not fit hulls already occupying slipways, which were separate from the dock facilities used for repair. In this timeline, three enlarged Tiger-derived ships already satisfy much of Fisher's demand for fast, heavy-gun vessels. Their presence makes it harder to sacrifice conventional battleships for another specialized battlecruiser programme.

evidence.note: Existing 15-inch-gun battlecruiser construction is linked to preserving the Revenge and Queen Elizabeth programmes and reducing the case for Fisher's large light cruisers.

segments.summary: Three large 15-inch-gun battlecruisers already under construction weaken Fisher's case for cancelling battleships to free resources for Courageous, Glorious, and Furious.

segments.title: Wartime performance makes battlecruiser retention credible
segments.body: Modern 15-inch-gun ships might keep David Beatty from moving his flag to Tiger and give the battlecruiser force a more suitable flagship. Without the historical HMAS Australia available at the outbreak of war, von Spee could turn toward Australia and meet Japanese Kongo-class ships sent south to intercept him. A stronger Jutland result, paired with Tiger's record at Dogger Bank, would support both fleet scouting and commerce protection. Carriers add scout aircraft to that system without automatically making battlecruisers redundant. This wartime record provides the political basis for seeking treaty retention.

evidence.note: The alternate wartime record combines Dogger Bank, Jutland, von Spee, and commerce protection into a retention case.

segments.summary: Better results at Jutland, continued value at Dogger Bank, and a plausible role against von Spee establish both fleet and commerce-protection arguments for retention.

segments.title: Washington creates a separate battlecruiser category
segments.body: The central diplomatic change replaces Washington's single capital-ship framework with separate battleship and battlecruiser categories. Britain and Japan could invoke trade protection, while the United States could accept the category because its Lexingtons were already under construction. The proposed limits are 40,000 tons for battlecruisers and 35,000 tons for battleships, with parallel 5:5:3-style allocations. Separate Dominion entitlements would formalize the prewar fleet-unit concept around local sea-lane defence. Negotiations would remain difficult because the United States could demand parity with the combined British and Dominion total. Discounting Dominion tonnage offers one possible compromise, although the exact figure is deliberately left open. These are bargaining assumptions within the scenario, not a claim that the historical ratios would transfer unchanged.

evidence.note: The transcript proposes separate treaty categories, tonnage limits, ratios, and Dominion allocations.

segments.summary: Retention requires separate treaty categories for battleships, battlecruisers, and aircraft carriers, with fast capital ships justified by their trade-protection role.

segments.title: Dominion ships replace some alliance reassurance
segments.body: The Dominion tonnage need not all be built immediately, and Canada could leave an allocation unused without transferring it to the Royal Navy. In the scenario, Canada also helps negotiate the end of the Anglo-Japanese Alliance. The same bargain lets Australia and New Zealand retain a tangible security guarantee as the alliance ends. Their 15-inch-gun ships would remain prestigious and militarily useful even if they ranked below treaty battleships. Local ownership ties regional reassurance directly to the treaty settlement.

evidence.note: Dominion allocations and the reassurance provided to Australia and New Zealand after the alliance are discussed.

segments.summary: Keeping modern battlecruisers gives Australia and New Zealand a visible security guarantee as the Anglo-Japanese Alliance ends.

segments.title: Japan reclassifies the Kongos and builds more Nagatos
segments.body: Reclassifying the four 27,500-ton Kongos removes roughly 110,000 tons from Japan's battleship total and places it inside a 120,000-ton battlecruiser allowance. Japan can therefore keep all four fast ships in the category, while rebuilding to the proposed 40,000-ton maximum would leave it with only three. The released battleship tonnage creates room for three improved Nagato-type ships. Washington becomes a managed opportunity for Japanese construction as well as a limit on overall strength.

evidence.note: The Kongo tonnage moves into the battlecruiser category and frees battleship allowance for improved Nagato-type construction.

segments.summary: Moving four Kongo-class ships into a separate battlecruiser allowance releases enough Japanese battleship tonnage for three improved Nagato-type ships.

segments.title: Five Lexingtons create an American fast wing
segments.body: The American battle line is already full, but five completed Lexington-class battlecruisers would supply the fast wing central to US scouting doctrine. Congress might dislike the expense yet still accept the ships as part of the treaty bargain, while using their existence to reject later requests for 8-inch-gun cruisers. Converting only the sixth Lexington leaves the Navy with one fast carrier and may force a slower battleship hull into a second carrier conversion. Japan could face a similar battlecruiser-and-battleship conversion pattern after earthquake damage, making carrier speed a new operational constraint for both navies.

evidence.note: Five Lexington battlecruisers, one fast carrier conversion, possible battleship-hull conversion, and the resulting scouting-force tradeoffs are discussed.

segments.summary: Completing five Lexington-class battlecruisers gives the US Navy the fast scouting force it wanted, but leaves only one fast hull available for carrier conversion.

segments.title: Speed defines the treaty battlecruiser category
segments.body: France has viable battlecruiser designs to consider, while Italy already has four fast Francesco Caracciolo-class hulls on the slips. Their eight 15-inch guns and projected 28-knot speed make at least two plausible candidates for completion inside a 40,000-ton battlecruiser limit. Under the proposed rule, a battlecruiser must make at least 28 knots, while a battleship can make any speed but must remain under 35,000 tons. Performance and tonnage would define the category instead of a navy's chosen label.

evidence.note: French design options, Italian Caracciolo completions, and a 28-knot performance boundary for treaty battlecruisers are proposed.

segments.summary: A 28-knot minimum and 40,000-ton ceiling let France consider dedicated designs and Italy classify fast Francesco Caracciolo-class ships as battlecruisers.

segments.title: A scheduled building system expands Dominion fleets
segments.body: Britain, Japan, and several Dominions would enter the agreement with unused tonnage, making a timed construction programme more workable than an absolute holiday. Britain could build battleships and battlecruisers in scheduled pairs while Japan adds ships one at a time. An Indian battlecruiser could be framed as recognition of wartime service, and Royal Navy personnel might help crew ships owned and funded by New Zealand or South Africa. Canada is the most likely to defer its entitlement until Pacific security concerns intensify in the late 1920s or 1930s.

evidence.note: The transcript outlines scheduled construction and the different Indian, South African, New Zealand, and Canadian cases.

segments.summary: Because several signatories begin below their allowances, Washington uses timed construction slots in place of a simple building holiday.

segments.title: Britain still needs County-class cruisers
segments.body: The revised capital-ship settlement would feed into a very different London Naval Treaty because the United States might enter the late 1920s with few heavy cruisers. Congress could point to the Lexingtons as powerful scouts and defer the Navy's request for Northampton-class 8-inch-gun cruisers. Britain would still build County-class cruisers because its postwar force had to cover global economic warfare, trade security, and an estimated requirement for roughly seventy cruisers. Battlecruisers and Dominion fleet units also need cruisers in their supporting squadrons, so American delay does not remove the Royal Navy's underlying requirement.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts delayed American heavy-cruiser demand with Britain's global cruiser and economic-security requirements.

segments.summary: Lexington battlecruisers may postpone American heavy cruisers, but Britain's global trade-protection and fleet-screening needs still drive County-class construction.

segments.title: Lexington-carrier pairs create early fast task forces
segments.body: A fast Lexington-class carrier could operate with one of its battlecruiser sisters as the core of an early American task force. The battlecruiser's 16-inch guns remove much of the rationale for mounting 8-inch guns on the carrier itself. Yorktown-class development could then grow around this fast formation, while a slower battleship-hull carrier supports the battle line. Giving the converted ships names such as United States or Washington would also attach unusual national prestige to naval aviation and make them especially prominent targets in any Pacific war.

evidence.note: A fast Lexington carrier-battlecruiser pairing, a slower battle-line carrier, Yorktown development, and carrier naming effects are explored.

segments.summary: Pairing a Lexington battlecruiser with the surviving fast carrier encourages a combined aviation-and-capital-ship doctrine before later Yorktown-class development.

segments.title: Britain builds three midsized battlecruisers
segments.body: British planners have about 99,300 tons of unused battlecruiser allowance under the proposed system. Two ships at the 40,000-ton ceiling would leave more than 13,000 tons unusable, whereas three vessels of roughly 33,100 tons consume almost the whole allocation. The ships would probably resemble the F3 concept and retain 15-inch guns. Combined with four new 35,000-ton battleships, that choice leaves the Royal Navy with six battlecruisers and eighteen battleships instead of concentrating its fast-ship tonnage in only two new hulls.

evidence.note: F3-like design choices, the 99,300-ton allowance, three 33,100-ton ships, and four additional battleships are calculated.

segments.summary: Britain can use nearly all its 99,300-ton allowance by dividing it among three roughly 33,100-ton F3-like battlecruisers.

segments.title: Different fast wings preserve Anglo-American parity
segments.body: The alternative settlement leaves the American and British core fleets near numerical parity while giving them different fast-wing structures. The United States has eighteen battleships and five maximum-size 40,000-ton Lexington-class battlecruisers. Britain has eighteen battleships and six smaller battlecruisers, while separate Dominion allocations expand the empire-wide total without putting every hull directly into the Royal Navy. A few French battlecruisers could also become prestige flagships, adding status competition to the fleet arithmetic.

evidence.note: The transcript compares eighteen-battleship British and American fleets, their differently sized battlecruiser forces, Dominion totals, and possible French prestige ships.

segments.summary: The treaty leaves Britain and the United States with eighteen battleships each, but their fast wings differ in ship size, numbers, and the place of Dominion forces.

segments.title: Italy favors new construction over reconstruction
segments.body: Italy's usable ship count depends on how the Francesco Caracciolo class is measured against an 80,000-ton allowance. An aggressive claim of roughly 26,000 tons standard displacement might squeeze in three ships, although their loading makes that figure doubtful. Even a smaller completion programme gives Italy a substantially stronger fast battle line. With treaty-approved construction available, later funds are more likely to go toward new ships than extensive reconstructions of older battleships.

evidence.note: Italian tonnage claims, possible Caracciolo completions, cost, and the shift from rebuilding old battleships to new construction are assessed.

segments.summary: Treaty permission to finish Francesco Caracciolo-class ships gives Italy a modern fast battle line and reduces the appeal of rebuilding older battleships.

segments.title: France and the Netherlands adopt commerce-protection ships
segments.body: France could use fast capital ships as the centre of a third major formation alongside its Mediterranean and Atlantic forces. Their likely purpose would be overseas imperial policing and commerce protection in the Far East. Once the treaty formally recognizes that mission, the Netherlands has a stronger reason to acquire a battlecruiser for the Dutch East Indies. A Dutch ship could come from a domestic project or a British, French, or Italian design. That would extend the category beyond the original signatories' main fleets.

evidence.note: French overseas fleet roles and a possible Dutch commerce-protection battlecruiser for the East Indies are proposed.

segments.summary: French battlecruisers become an overseas imperial-policing force, while the Netherlands gains a reason to acquire a comparable ship for the East Indies.

segments.title: New battleships give Japan a treaty success
segments.body: Japan still receives a 3:5 relationship instead of the 7:10 ratio many advocates wanted. The revised settlement also permits new battleships, giving the navy a concrete achievement to claim from the conference. Those ships offer visible status and a focus for naval pride, which could make the treaty appear less purely restrictive. Greater confidence does not excuse later aggression. In this scenario, it changes one of the insecurity-driven traps that shaped interwar decision-making.

evidence.note: New treaty construction is connected to Japanese naval pride, international status, confidence, and later strategic decision-making.

segments.summary: Although Japan still accepts an inferior ratio, permission to build new battleships gives the navy a concrete achievement around which to rally status and confidence.

segments.title: Dominion capital ships demand local naval infrastructure
segments.body: With their own capital ships, Australia and New Zealand would rely less on distant imperial forces for reassurance. The ships would become a focus for modernization and growth in each Dominion navy. Keeping them operational requires supporting forces, trained personnel, dockyard capacity, and other infrastructure throughout the 1920s and 1930s. If war still begins in 1939, that long preparation leaves both navies materially different from their historical counterparts.

evidence.note: Dominion ownership, confidence, naval growth, and the infrastructure investment needed before a possible 1939 war are linked.

segments.summary: Retained battlecruisers give Australia and New Zealand a fleet cornerstone and require sustained investment in the people and facilities needed to operate it.

segments.title: Fast capital ships disrupt German rearmament
segments.body: Germany would confront larger British, American, French, Italian, and Japanese fleets before beginning its own rearmament. Numerous fast capital ships make the Deutschland-class commerce-raider concept far less attractive, because even France can deploy ships capable of hunting them. If Germany does not build the Deutschlands, it may also lack the industrial progression needed to produce the Scharnhorst class and then the Bismarck class on the historical timetable. The same altered balance could push the Soviet Union toward capital ships earlier, making the familiar naval setting of the Second World War increasingly unlikely.

evidence.note: Larger treaty fleets are linked to the viability of the Deutschland, Scharnhorst, and Bismarck programmes and to earlier Soviet capital-ship ambitions.

segments.summary: A world crowded with Allied battlecruisers weakens the German commerce-raider strategy and may redirect both German and Soviet capital-ship programmes.

segments.title: Dominion carriers accelerate naval aviation
segments.body: If aircraft carriers share the commerce-protection justification used for battlecruisers, each Dominion could receive up to 27,000 tons of carrier capacity. Governments might choose one large armoured carrier or divide the allowance between two improved Hermes-sized ships, creating a broad family of light-fleet-carrier-like vessels before 1939. With smaller carriers distributed around the empire, the Royal Navy would have more reason to concentrate on large fleet carriers and forward aviation support ships such as Unicorn. The wider construction base would also bring more navies into carrier operations, aircraft development, and practical bombing experience. The scenario still depends on one earlier result: modern 15-inch-gun battlecruisers must prove enough wartime value to make treaty retention credible.

evidence.note: The transcript explores Dominion carrier allowances, improved Hermes-sized ships, larger Royal Navy carriers, and aviation support vessels.
The conclusion restates that proven wartime value and 15-inch-gun ships are necessary for treaty retention.

segments.summary: Parallel carrier entitlements could produce large Dominion carriers or pairs of improved Hermes-sized ships and push the Royal Navy toward larger fleet carriers.
